To address these challenges, this paper introduces a Split Federated Learning framework combined with a multi-task transformer-based model designed to address two critical tasks: battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation. The framework uses a uniﬁed approach, leveraging a single model for both tasks, which simpliﬁes deployment and reduces operational complexity. This approach eliminates the need for training and maintaining separate models for each task, resulting in signiﬁcant practical and computational beneﬁts. The proposed framework employs a hierarchical federated learning architecture that integrates EVs, edge servers at charging stations, and a global server in the cloud. By using federated learning principles, sensitive data remains localized at the EV level, safeguarding privacy while enabling collaborative training across distributed nodes. Furthermore, the hierarchical design coordinates learning across multiple levels, ensuring model consistency and scalability. The use of split learning further enhances the system’s efﬁciency by dividing the model into segments, with only the initial layers being trained locally on the EV, while the rest are processed on the edge server. This design minimizes computational demands on EVs, making the framework suitable for resource-constrained devices. Another critical advantage of this approach is the optimization of training sessions during the EV’s charging periods. By performing training while the EV is connected to the charging station, the framework avoids depleting the battery for computational tasks, preserving energy for essential functionalities. These design considerations make the proposed solution practical and efﬁcient, aligning with the energy and privacy requirements of modern EV systems. To summarize, the main contributions of this paper are: performance over state-of-the-art methods for both battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation tasks. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews the related work. Section III details the development and operation of the proposed framework. Section IV presents the performance evaluation results along with a comparative analysis against state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.

sections.title: RELATED WORK
paragraphs: Battery diagnostics and capacity estimation are critical research areas for ensuring the safety, reliability, and operational efﬁciency of electric vehicles (EVs). Early approaches often relied on statistical models and traditional machine learning techniques, such as statistical distribution analysis and canonical algorithms, to diagnose faults and detect anomalies [5], [6]. More recently, Li et al. [7] review artiﬁcial neural network (ANN) approaches for state-of-health (SoH) estimation and remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, discussing battery aging mechanisms, available datasets, and ANN architectures, and outlining key challenges related to deployment feasibility and model interpretability. Sultan et al. [8] propose an active cell balancing system to address imbalanced state of charge (SoC) in EV lithium-ion battery packs caused by cell inconsistencies. The study evaluates seven machine learning models for predicting battery lifespan and remaining useful life (RUL). Das et al. [9] estimate the state of health (SoH) of lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles using machine learning algorithms like KNN, SVR, DT, and RF, based on direct battery measurements (voltage, current, temperature). The study proposes collaboration with hardware manufacturers for better battery health monitoring systems. The advent of deep learning introduced advanced models [10], such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, capable of capturing temporal dependencies and improving anomaly detection in battery systems [6], [11]. However, the development of robust deep learning methods hinges on the availability of large-scale, publicly accessible datasets. In response, recent advancements in EV battery research have produced datasets tailored to various tasks, including anomaly detection, capacity estimation, and remaining useful life (RUL) prediction. For instance, datasets such as Sultan et al. [8] and HUST [12] focus on controlled experimental conditions, while large-scale datasets like EVBattery [1] provide diverse real-world charging data. Additionally, specialized datasets address manufacturing defects through CT scans [13] or explore capacity estimation using voltage relaxation pro- ﬁles [14]. Xiong et al. [15] propose a lithium-ion battery health prognosis method using real-world BMS in electric vehicles. The approach combines partial charge voltage curves as health indicators with a moving-window-based RUL prediction model. While the method is well-suited for many applications, its reliance on linear degradation models may present challenges when applied to batteries exhibiting complex degradation patterns.
AMARA KORBA et al.: SMTFL FOR BATTERY HEALTH AND CAPACITY ESTIMATION IN EVs 3

Deng et al. [16] propose a rapid health estimation framework for in-service EV battery packs that combines a digital-twin model based on an equivalent-circuit representation, feature extraction from short charging segments, and deep convolutional neural networks with transfer learning and domain adaptation to cope with limited labeled ﬁeld data. Han et al. [17] emphasize the signiﬁcance of dynamically reconﬁgurable battery management systems (RBSs) for enhancing fault tolerance, improving charge and temperature balancing, and achieving greater energy efﬁciency and operational ﬂexibility. While the proposed approach offers valuable advancements, the implementation of RBSs may encounter challenges such as the computational demands of optimization algorithms, increased hardware design requirements, and practical considerations like managing transient behaviors during switch operations.

Liu et al. [18] tackle the challenge of battery state of health (SoH) estimation under limited sample conditions by introducing a reﬁned composite multiscale discrete sine entropy (RCMDSE) algorithm. Similarly, Kumari et al. [19] propose a hybrid approach for estimating state of charge, health, and temperature (SoC, SoH, SoT). Their method combines an emperor penguin-based residual network-110 (R110) with bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM) networks. This approach demonstrates signiﬁcant promise, achieving high accuracy on EV drive cycles simulated in MATLAB. However, the reliance on advanced optimization techniques, such as simulated annealing, may limit its real-time applicability in resource-constrained environments. Kant et al., [20] proposed a method that integrates a bidirectional recurrent neural network and long-short-term memory (biRNN-LSTM) to improve the prediction of the state of health (SoH) by identifying complex patterns and improving accuracy.

Despite notable advancements in battery diagnostics andcapacity estimation, several limitations persist within the state of the art. Approaches targeting complex degradation behaviors often fail to capture nonlinear dynamics [8], while recent innovations [17], [19] face challenges related to computational overhead, limiting real-time applicability in resource-constrained EV. Many methods rely on datasets generated under controlled laboratory conditions [6], [11], restricting their generalizability to diverse real-world scenarios. Moreover, existing techniques often assume that EV data can be centrally collected, overlooking critical privacy concerns.

Federated learning (FL) has recently gained traction asa distributed training paradigm in a variety of application domains. For instance, Wu et al. [21] employ federated deep reinforcement learning to perform multi-objective optimization in STAR-RIS-aided satellite–aerial–ground integrated networks (SAGINs). In the context of battery health monitoring and state-of-health (SoH) estimation, several studies [22], [23], [24] have leveraged FL-based designs. Abbaraju and Kundu [22] propose a federated ensemble learning (FEL) approach that combines federated learning and ensemble learning to enhance SoH estimation. Their solution relies on an LSTM model that is updated after each trip, leveraging heterogeneous data sources such as trafﬁc conditions and weather.

Wang et al. [23] introduce an adaptive multi-personalized federated learning (AMFL) algorithm that reﬁnes SoH estimation by dynamically adjusting local models through personalized layers and client clustering while incorporating a differential privacy mechanism. Similarly, Wong et al. [24] develop a decentralized federated learning approach for Li-ion battery SoH forecasting, featuring an improved client selection strategy and real-world validation experiments.

Despite notable progress, existing battery diagnostic methods exhibit several limitations. Model-based approaches often rely on simpliﬁed linear degradation assumptions [15], failing to capture complex real-world aging dynamics. Federated learning (FL) methods for SoH estimation [22], [23], [24] reduce data centralization but impose signiﬁcant computational burdens on resource-constrained EVs and lack energy-efﬁcient training schedules, which could impact battery autonomy. Moreover, they typically focus on a single task (e.g., SoH estimation), requiring separate models for different diagnostics and increasing system complexity. Many methods are also evaluated on controlled laboratory datasets [6], [11], limiting their applicability to diverse real-world conditions.

To address these gaps, we propose a Split Multi-Task Federated Learning (SMTFL) framework that: (1) employs a Transformer-based encoder to model nonlinear temporal dependencies; (2) reduces on-device computation by ofﬂoading heavy layers to edge infrastructure via split learning, where only early layers are trained locally; (3) incorporates differential privacy mechanisms to protect sensitive battery data during model updates; (4) uniﬁes battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation into a single model, eliminating the need for separate, task-speciﬁc models and optimizing parameter efﬁciency; (5) schedules training exclusively during charging sessions to preserve EV battery life; and (6) is validated on the large-scale real-world EVBattery dataset [1] to ensure practical relevance. This innovative framework effectively balances scalability, privacy preservation, and computational efﬁciency, addressing the key challenges identiﬁed in the state of the art.

sections.title: SMTFL FRAMEWORK
paragraphs: Our framework integrates split learning and federatedarchitectures for battery health monitoring, balancing local computation with global performance while incorporating differential privacy. The following sections detail the architectural components, including the split Transformer model, privacy-preserving training protocol, and federated coordination strategy.

Our framework integrates split learning and federatedarchitectures for battery health monitoring, balancing local computation with global performance while incorporating differential privacy. The following sections detail the architectural components, including the split Transformer model, privacy-preserving training protocol, and federated coordination strategy.

subsections.title: System Model
paragraphs: The proposed system employs a hierarchical federatedlearning architecture that integrates three primary components: electric vehicles (EVs) as clients, edge servers deployed at charging stations, and a global parameter server in the cloud. The workﬂow is designed to ensure synchronization, prevent version conﬂicts, and facilitate efﬁcient and scalable model training. Figure 1 illustrates the interactions and hierarchical structure among these components. At the start of each global

round, the cloud server distributes the global model to edge servers located within charging stations, which then propagate it to connected EVs. Each edge server collects model updates from EVs during a station-level Aggregation Time Window (ATW), performs local aggregation, and forwards the result to the cloud server. The cloud operates within a longer Synchronization Window (SW) to gather updates from all edge servers, execute global aggregation, and redistribute the reﬁned model.

The SMTFL framework leverages Power Line Communication (PLC) over the charging cable, standardized in ISO 15118 [25], to transmit model updates and intermediate representations (smashed data) between EVs and edge servers. This approach eliminates separate communication hardware, reduces system complexity, and enhances security by utilizing the naturally isolated channel of the charging cable. The physical connection serves a dual purpose: power transfer and data exchange. Communication is secured with mutual Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 [26], ensuring conﬁdentiality, integrity, and authenticity. Charging stations communicate with the cloud server via standard Internet connections (e.g., ﬁber, 4G/5G), enabling reliable transmission of aggregated updates and global model distribution.

and the station’s capacity (Nmax). The goal is to determine the number of EVs utilizing the station within the ATW while accounting for constraints such as the limited number of charging points and varying levels of station utilization.

The arrival of EVs at a charging station is modeled as a Poisson process with average arrival rate \lambdaEV (EVs per unit time). During an ATW of duration TAT W, the total expected arrivals is Narrivals = \lambdaEV · TAT W. The actual number of EVs simultaneously connected during the ATW is inﬂuenced by Tsession, Nmax, and an occupation factor \rho (fraction of charging points typically in use):
\rho · Tsession · Narrivals, Nmax

When the station is underutilized, Nconnected is limited byarrival rate and session duration; when saturated, it is capped by Nmax. The total number of EVs utilizing the station during the ATW, denoted NEV , combines these effects:

This formulation ensures the total is bounded by both arrivalrate and station capacity for concurrent charging sessions.

In practice, EVs may not complete local training or transmitupdates simultaneously within an ATW due to varying computational loads or intermittent connectivity. The edge server aggregates all updates received by the window’s deadline; EVs that miss the cutoff participate in the subsequent ATW.
AMARA KORBA et al.: SMTFL FOR BATTERY HEALTH AND CAPACITY ESTIMATION IN EVs 5

The subsequent SW at the cloud level provides additional buffering, allowing edge servers to forward aggregated models without requiring strict synchronization. Moreover, if an EV disconnects prematurely, it can resume training in a later session by downloading the latest global model. This design ensures robust operation under realistic, asynchronous update patterns and connectivity variations, making the system practical for real-world deployment.

subsections.title: Prediction Model Architecture
paragraphs: The prediction model employs a Transformer encoder toprocess multivariate time-series data, performing two critical tasks in parallel: battery health anomaly detection (binary classiﬁcation) and capacity estimation (regression). The Transformer encoder is selected for its superior ability to capture long-range temporal dependencies, which are essential for accurate battery diagnostics. The model comprises six encoder layers, each containing a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a feed-forward network. In our split learning conﬁguration, the architecture is divided at a preciseboundary: the ﬁrst two encoder layers form the client-side (EV) component, while the remaining four layers, along with global pooling and task-speciﬁc heads, constitute the server-side (edge) component. This split follows established privacy–complexity trade-offs in split learning [27]: early layers extract low-level features with minimal privacy risk, while deeper, computationally intensive layers are ofﬂoadedto the edge server. During operation, the EV processes raw data through the ﬁrst two layers, producing intermediate activations (smashed data) of dimension [batch_size, sequence_length=128, d_model=64], which aretransmitted to the edge server.

subsections.title: Split Federated Training
paragraphs: The client-side model processes raw battery data locally, transforming it into intermediate representations (smashed data). To preserve privacy, Gaussian noise is added to the smashed data before transmission, ensuring differential privacy. The noisy smashed data are then sent to the edge server, which completes the forward pass using its layers, computes the multi-task loss, and backpropagates gradients through its own layers and back to the smashed data. These gradients are returned to the EV, which uses them to update its local layers via backpropagation. After completing a ﬁxed number of local epochs, the EV uploads its updated client-side weights, again applying differential privacy by adding Gaussian noise, to the edge server for aggregation. This design reduces the computational load on EVs while safeguarding data privacy and ensuring scalable, distributed training.

subsections.title: EVBattery Dataset
paragraphs: We evaluate our framework using the EVBattery dataset [1], a large-scale real-world benchmark for EV battery diagnostics. The dataset comprises charging snippets collected under diverse conditions—including fast/slow charging and varying temperatures—from three anonymized manufacturers. Each record contains 128-step time-series of eight features (voltage, current, temperature, SOC, etc.) and meta-information (vehicle ID, mileage, snippet index). Binary health labels (0: normal, 1: anomaly) and continuous capacity labels (28.28–46.23 Ah) accompany each sample. A full description is given in Table I; additional dataset speciﬁcs are available in the original publication [1].

The cleaned dataset contained no missing values. To preserve real-world conditions, the natural class imbalance was maintained for anomaly detection; in Non-IID splits, each client was guaranteed at least three-batch-size samples per class to prevent extreme skew, without any synthetic resampling. This approach ensures a realistic evaluation of the model under practical data distributions.

The dataset was prepared from raw .pkl ﬁles containingmultivariate time-series data and metadata. Sequences were converted into NumPy arrays, and entries with missing or invalid values were discarded. Valid capacity labels (non-zero) were retained as regression targets, while anomaly labels were encoded as binary values (0: normal, 1: anomalies such as lithium plating or thermal runaway). For normalization, all time-series features were standardized per feature (zero mean, unit variance) using a StandardScaler ﬁtted exclusively on the training set. Capacity labels were similarly normalized.

subsections.title: Implementation & Experimental Results
paragraphs: The architectural details and hyperparameters of the Transformer model are summarized in Table II. The model was

implemented in Python 3.9 using the PyTorch 2.0 deep learning framework. It comprises a stack of six encoder layers, each consisting of an 8-head self-attention mechanism and a feed-forward network with 128-dimensional hidden states. The input data is projected into a 64-dimensional embedding space and enriched with sinusoidal positional encodings to retain temporal information. The loss function combines binary cross-entropy for anomaly detection and mean squared error for capacity estimation to ensure effective training across tasks. For privacy protection, Gaussian differential privacy was applied with noise scale \sigma = 0.3, gradient norm bound C = 2.0, and \delta = 10−5. Additionally, smashed data were perturbed with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.01 before transmission. All experiments were conducted on a workstation equipped with an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU with 48 GB of memory.

To simulate realistic federated learning scenarios wheredata distributions vary across clients, we implement a labelskew partitioning strategy for Non-IID (Non-Independent and Non-Identically Distributed) experiments. Each EV client is assigned a dominant class (class 0, normal samples) while ensuring a minimum of 3× batch size samples from the minority class (class 1, anomalies). This approach creates heterogeneous local data distributions, reﬂecting real-world conditions where certain EV clients may observe more frequent anomalies than others. Table III presents the resulting sample distribution across 20 EVs for a representative run, clearly showing the label-skew while maintaining the minimum-sample constraint for both classes.
We validate our evaluation using 5-fold cross-validation.

To ensure robust assessment, the folds are constructed with a strict temporal order: within each fold, the training data strictly precedes the test data in time, eliminating temporal data leakage. Additionally, we ensure that no EV client (identiﬁed by unique vehicle IDs) is shared between the training and test sets of any fold, preventing cross-client leakage and guaranteeing complete isolation between model development and evaluation data.

As expected, a constant and stable participation yields thebest performance, as evidenced by the results in Table VI.

Although this scenario is rare in practice, it establishes a solid baseline. Under high-density conditions, simulating urban environments with heavy trafﬁc, performance remains exceptionally close to the ideal, with an anomaly-detection accuracy of 98.95% (Non-IID) and a capacity-estimation MAE of 0.3394 Ah, conﬁrming that the framework can operate at a near-optimal level in dense EV networks.

Conversely, the low-density scenario, representative of ruralareas or off-peak periods, leads to a measurable but limited drop in performance. For anomaly detection, accuracy decreases slightly to 98.50% (F1-score = 97.97%), corresponding to a reduction of 0.58 percentage points. Capacity estimation is more affected, with the MAE rising to 0.3616 Ah (NRMSE = 0.0628), which represents an approximate 15.2% relative increase compared to the ideal-case MAE (0.3139 Ah). This modest degradation is further illustrated in Figures 4d, 4e and 4f, which plot the evolution of MAE, MSE, and RMSE across the training rounds. The curves conﬁrm that, despite higher round-to-round variability, the error metrics remain bounded and converge to values consistent with those reported in Table VI. Nevertheless, even under this challenging conﬁguration, the results remain excellent and operationally viable: anomaly detection retains an accuracy above 98.5% and capacity estimation exhibits a mean absolute error below 0.37 Ah, which corresponds to an uncertainty of less than 2 km in remaining range (assuming a consumption of 0.2 Ah/km). This demonstrates the robustness of the SMTFL framework in the face of realistic participation ﬂuctuations in electric-vehicle ﬂeets.

subsections.title: Comparative Analysis
paragraphs: We evaluate our framework against both centralized andfederated baselines to contextualize its performance. Although battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation have been studied in the literature, to the best of our knowledge, only [1] utilized the EVBattery dataset, enabling a direct comparison. Notably, the authors of [1] employed multiple machine learning methods, providing a valuable opportunity to benchmark our solution against various approaches. However, their work did not incorporate federated learning (FL). Therefore, we implemented FL-based baselines (LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU) to compare our solution against FL methods as well. Figure 5 illustrates the performance comparison of our solution with centralized ML models from [1] for both tasks: AUROC for Task 1 (battery health anomaly detection) and RMSE for Task 2 (battery capacity estimation). These metrics were not selected arbitrarily but were adopted because [1] exclusively relied on them, ensuring a consistent and meaningful comparison.

The AUROC scores demonstrate a clear improvementachieved by the proposed models (MTFL and SMTFL). While traditional methods such as AE, Deep SVDD, and LSTMAD exhibit moderate performance, our models signiﬁcantly outperform them, reaching an AUROC of 99.9%, marking a

substantial advancement in battery health anomaly detection. For the capacity estimation task, evaluated through RMSE, the proposed models also show superior performance. Baseline methods such as Random Forest, XGBoost, and GCNN achieve RMSE values ranging from 1.39 to 1.42, indicating limitations in accurately predicting capacity under complex conditions. In contrast, the proposed models achieve RMSE values of 0.64 and 0.66, respectively, signiﬁcantly reducing the prediction error. The strong performance of SMTFL can be attributed to its ability to effectively capture multivariate temporal dependencies and feature interactions, leveraging the advanced Transformer-based architecture integrated into the federated learning framework.

distribution. Baseline models (FL-LSTM, FL-BiLSTM, FL- GRU) yield accuracies around 0.96–0.97 and MAEs around 0.46–0.48. Our FL-Transformer (non-split) notably improves both tasks (accuracy 0.988, MAE 0.326). The proposed SMTFL (split) achieves the best accuracy (0.989), F1-score (0.985), and MAE (0.322), while the non-split variant attains the lowest RMSE (0.647). The slight increase in RMSE for the split model may reﬂect the added noise from the split process. Our SMTFL framework not only uniﬁes anomaly detection and capacity estimation within a single model while ofﬂoading heavy computation to the edge, but also delivers superior performance compared to recurrent baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Transformer architecture with split learning in federated multi-task settings.

substantial advancement in battery health anomaly detection. For the capacity estimation task, evaluated through RMSE, the proposed models also show superior performance. Baseline methods such as Random Forest, XGBoost, and GCNN achieve RMSE values ranging from 1.39 to 1.42, indicating limitations in accurately predicting capacity under complex conditions. In contrast, the proposed models achieve RMSE values of 0.64 and 0.66, respectively, signiﬁcantly reducing the prediction error. The strong performance of SMTFL can be attributed to its ability to effectively capture multivariate temporal dependencies and feature interactions, leveraging the advanced Transformer-based architecture integrated into the federated learning framework.

Our FL-Transformer (non-split) notably improves both tasks (accuracy 0.988, MAE 0.326). The proposed SMTFL (split) achieves the best accuracy (0.989), F1-score (0.985), and MAE (0.322), while the non-split variant attains the lowest RMSE (0.647). The slight increase in RMSE for the split model may reﬂect the added noise from the split process. Our SMTFL framework not only uniﬁes anomaly detection and capacity estimation within a single model while ofﬂoading heavy computation to the edge, but also delivers superior performance compared to recurrent baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Transformer architecture with split learning in federated multi-task settings.

sections.title: CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
paragraphs: This paper introduced a Split Multi-Task Federated Learning (SMTFL) framework for joint battery health anomaly detection and capacity estimation in electric vehicles (EVs). The proposed approach combines a Transformer-based encoder with a split federated architecture to achieve state-of-the-art performance while addressing critical challenges in scalability, privacy, and energy efﬁciency. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods, achieving an accuracy of 98.9% for anomaly detection and a MAE of 0.32 for capacity estimation. These results validate the model’s capability to capture complex temporal dependencies and feature interactions across both tasks. By enabling EVs to train a single uniﬁed model locally and ofﬂoading heavy computations to edge servers, the SMTFL framework signiﬁcantly reduces on-device resource requirements. Moreover, privacy is preserved through differential privacy mechanisms and split

learning, while training is scheduled exclusively during charging sessions to minimize energy overhead. Collectively, these attributes make the SMTFL framework a practical and efﬁcient solution for large-scale, privacy-aware EV battery diagnostics. Future work will focus on extending the framework to additional battery management system (BMS) tasks, such as predicting battery lifespan and identifying speciﬁc component failures. We also plan to explore adaptive split points that dynamically adjust the computation ofﬂoading based on device capabilities and network conditions, as well as design more sophisticated multitask models that integrate a broader set of BMS functions without compromising efﬁciency.
